newsitem.title: GREECE: Simitis wants to reform Greece, but can he?.
newsitem.headline: Simitis wants to reform Greece, but can he?.

text.p: Socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis, who will announce his new cabinet on Tuesday, wants to use a strong election win to change the face of Greece with a cabinet of hard-nosed reformers.
But the strong showing of socialist party hardliners in Sunday's election may prove his main hurdle, officials said.

"We now expect that top ministries will be given more or less to the same people because they did very well in Sunday's election. Simitis wants deep reforms but it won't be easy," a member of his former cabinet told Reuters.

Officials said Simitis's early plans for a new-look cabinet had receded. He received a mandate to form the new government on Monday and is expected to announce his team on Tuesday evening at 18.00 hrs local (1500 GMT).

He now looks set to use the same ministers but shuffled among top posts and to keep his economic team intact -- Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou, Finance Minister Alexandros Papadopoulos and Development Minister Vasso Papandreou.

They are credited with slashing inflation from double digits to 8.5 percent in August and attacking tax evasion but are reserved on privatisations and have a poor record in attracting foreign investments.

Two private casinos, among the most important foreign investments in the past two years, fought with Papandreou who wants to impose restrictions on their operation by altering already signed contracts.

Simitis will also include in his new cabinet former Interior Minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos and Defence Minister Gerassimos Arsenis, his two defeated rivals in the race to replace late party founder Andreas Papandreou at the helm of of the party and government.
Both pledged in a party congress in June to safeguard socialist policies and analysts said they would resist moves by Simitis for reform.
Simitis has called for "leaps ahead" after many years of stagnant socialist rule, mainly due to Papandreou's poor health, but has not said how he will do it.
"If he wants to reform Greece he must first reform the way the socialist party thinks and operates. This is a big challenge," the official said.
Simitis wants to bring Greeece in line with its European Union partners with higher growth rates so that it joins the European Monetary Union sometime after 1999.
But to do this he must confine a huge and unproductive public sector, close down or sell indebted state companies like Olympic Airways and give brave initiatives to the private sector.
"In a nutshell he must do everything the traditional socialist party once fought against," the official said.
